newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Pictet ups UBS, cuts CS to hold.
newsitem.headline: Pictet ups UBS, cuts CS to hold.

text.p: Pictet & Cie upgraded Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) from hold to buy based on potential revenue and earnings growth.
The Geneva-based private bank also lowered Credit Suisse Group from buy to hold, saying the shares were already near year-end price targets and broadly discounted likely benefits from restructuring.
Pictet said UBS was best positioned of the three big Swiss banks achieve sustained earnings growth from a restructuring of Swiss retail business that all three have started.
"In addition, we are detecting signs that maybe management at UBS is now starting to focus more on shareholders and value creation," Pictet wrote in a weekly Swiss equity review.

Pictet said UBS seemed to be the most advanced in trimming costly Swiss retail business and had good management information tools in place, giving it an advantage over its rivals in increasing revenue.
"The market appears to be underestimating revenue and earnings growth potential," the private bank said.
Pictet also said UBS, which for years traded at a premium, now had the lowest valuation of the three big Swiss bank shares -- UBS, Credit Suisse and Swiss Bank Corp (SBC).
Pictet raised its estimate of UBS earnings per share (EPS) from this year to 106.8 Swiss francs per bearer from an earlier 100.1.
EPS in 1998 should now be 121.3 Swiss francs as against an earlier forecast of 111.9.
Pictet set a 12-month target price for UBS bearer shares of 1,600 Swiss francs. The share closed at 1,353 on Monday.
Credit Suisse Group on the other hand had already nearly reached Pictet's year-end price target of 170 to 180 Swiss francs per registered share.
The share closed on Monday at 163.75 and hit a year high of 176.50 on March 12.

Pictet said Credit Suisse had once offered the greatest potential for restrucuring because it had not fully integrated major acquisitions before announcing a major streamlining and cost reduction program last year.
"We believe that the shares are now fairly valued and broadly discount likely benefits from the cost-reduction program," Pictet said.
